doc.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023

chapter: Army, Chicago and the new music
title: Hearing Albert Ayler, Coltrane and Chicago's McKie Fitzhugh's club
summary: Asked about 1961, he recalls hearing Albert Ayler in Europe, then Coltrane's Impulse album in Chicago, and the weekend big names and weekday sessions with Eddie Buster's trio at McKie Fitzhugh's.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: All right. I want to take you back a little bit before that and I read that in 1961 you had what this review said, a hard bop group and Joseph Jarman and Anthony Braxton. My question is at that point, in 1961, Coltrane released “My Favorite Things” and Ornette Coleman “Free Jazz,” Max Roach had a “Freedom Suite,” and one of my favorites, Hank Mobley had an LP called “Roll Call.” Was there decision-making for you at that point in your career about your direction?

Well you know like yeah, I had, we had times that we would all go to Berlin to join with the Berlin band there and also the band from Orleans, France was there as well. And who should be in the band from Orleans, France but Albert Ayler you know. And Albert, I heard him way back then and the way I chose the saxophone is what is your sound you know, where is your sound you know. Because all the great players, you know they had a sound that they were pursuing you know. But when I heard Albert you know I didn’t know what he was doing but I understood that he had an enormous sound on the instrument you know. So he won me over like right away. I didn’t — like I said — I didn’t understand exactly what he was doing but he had me there. And like it wasn’t until I came back into Chicago, you know, was out of the Army and heard Coltrane doing that album called “Coltrane” on Impulse where he did “Inch Worm” and “Out of this World” and all this stuff with the band that he had with McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison. So I thought wow, you mean you can do that or you can do this? ‘Cause it was a different approach of improvisation in terms of a modal concept you know. And so I paid attention to that and you know in Chicago too there was McKie Fitzhugh’s Club on 64th and Cottage Grove, between 64th and 63rd on Cottage Grove, and there you know on the weekends you go up in there and man, Dexter Gordon, John Coltrane, I mean John Coltrane come to Chicago he had so many dinner invitations. I mean there’s no way in the world he could have made all of those you know. So I — just a minute let’s see now — I paid attention to that and then during the weekdays they had a local trio, Eddie Buster and the trio that he played with, and you know, and it was a lot of sessioning going on. And then I was going to the sessions and playing and then I kept hearing this strange music you know and I told Eddie I said man I’m hearing this, I’m hearing that, and so he encouraged me to keep moving on that you know? And when I did that then it started kind of like pouring out of me and then you know they were all right there encouraging me to do it.
